title: U.S. House · New York's 18th Congressional District
area: Mid-Hudson Valley, covering Ulster County and Orange County and part of Dutchess County, north of New York City.

context.text: Both parties' primaries were canceled: incumbent Pat Ryan advanced unopposed on the Democratic and Working Families Party lines, and Jackie Auringer advanced unopposed on the Republican and Conservative Party lines after Sharanjit Thind withdrew from both. As of September 22, 2026, Cook Political Report and Inside Elections rated the general election "Solid Democratic" and Decision Desk and Sabato's Crystal Ball rated it "Safe Democratic." A late-July 2026 poll sponsored by the Ryan campaign (Global Strategy Group) showed Ryan leading Auringer 53%-39%.

candidates.name: Pat Ryan
candidates.currentRole: U.S. Representative for NY-18 (since 2022; represented NY-19 2022-2023)

summary.text: Pat Ryan is the incumbent Democratic U.S. Representative for New York's 18th Congressional District. A West Point graduate and Army intelligence officer who served two combat tours in Iraq, he worked in the technology sector and was Ulster County Executive from 2019 to 2022. He won a 2022 special election in the old NY-19 and was elected to the redrawn NY-18 that November; he sits on the Armed Services and Transportation and Infrastructure committees.

background.text: Born and raised in Kingston, New York, and graduated from Kingston High School in 2000; his official biography calls him a fifth-generation Hudson Valley native.
Earned a bachelor's degree in international politics from the U.S. Military Academy at West Point in 2004 and a master's degree in security studies from Georgetown University (2013, per Ballotpedia).
Served in the U.S. Army from 2004 to 2009 as a military intelligence officer; his official biography says he served two combat tours in Iraq and earned two Bronze Stars.

After the Army, worked as deputy director of Berico Technologies, co-founded the software company Praescient Analytics in 2011, and was a senior vice president at Dataminr from 2015 to 2017, according to Wikipedia.
Ran in the 2018 Democratic primary in NY-19, receiving 18% to Antonio Delgado's 22%.

Won an April 2019 special election for Ulster County Executive, took office June 7, 2019, and won a full term in November 2019; he resigned on September 9, 2022. His official biography says he led the county through the COVID-19 pandemic and the redevelopment of the former IBM site, now iPark 87.

Won the August 23, 2022 special election in NY-19 over Dutchess County Executive Marc Molinaro, 51.1%-48.8%, and was sworn in September 13, 2022; in November 2022 he won the redrawn NY-18, defeating Republican Colin Schmitt.

In the House he serves on the Armed Services Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, and his official biography describes him as the first West Point graduate to represent the Academy in the U.S. House.
Lives in Gardiner with his wife, Rebecca, and their two sons, according to his official biography.

positions.summary: Official issues page describes him as a member of the Congressional Pro Choice Caucus who backs legislation to codify a right to abortion care and access to mifepristone.
positions.quote: As a proud member of the Congressional Pro Choice Caucus, I champion legislation like the EACH Act to ensure affordable access to abortion care, Abortion is Health Care Everywhere Act, and the Women’s Health Protection Act, that codifies a woman’s right to make her own reproductive healthcare choices and the ability of healthcare providers to offer them.

positions.summary: Official issues page says he backs an assault weapons ban, safe-storage law, enhanced background checks and a federal red-flag law.
positions.quote: I will keep pushing for common sense gun reform like the Enhanced Background Checks Act, the Federal Extreme Risk Protection Order Act, and the Stopping the Fraudulent Sales of Firearms Act to keep illicit guns out of the hands of criminals who shouldn’t have them.

record.text: Serves on the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee (Highways and Transit; Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials; Water Resources and Environment subcommittees) and the House Armed Services Committee (Cyber, Information Technologies, and Innovation; Intelligence and Special Operations subcommittees) in the 119th Congress (2025-2026).
Won the August 23, 2022 special election for the old NY-19 seat over Marcus Molinaro, 51.4% to 48.5%, before winning election to the redrawn NY-18 that November.

summary.text: Jackie Auringer is the Republican and Conservative Party nominee for NY-18, having advanced unopposed after both primaries were canceled. She was raised in Kingston, works in her family's construction business and in marketing, and describes herself as a mental health advocate who has done community and campaign work. Her campaign says she is running on affordability, accountability and opportunity.

background.text: Auringer was born and raised in Kingston, in Ulster County, according to her campaign website.
She earned a marketing degree from the Lutgert College of Business, according to her campaign website.
She works in her family's construction business as a project manager and managerial accountant, and also works as a marketing and branding professional, according to her campaign website.

Her campaign website says she is a philanthropist who has been involved in charitable, community and civic efforts as well as political campaigns, including voter outreach and grassroots organizing, and that she is an advocate for mental health.
Her campaign website says she is not a career politician and quotes New York State Republican Party Chairman Ed Cox in support of her candidacy.

priorities.text: Says she would focus on affordability, government accountability, and creating economic opportunity in the Hudson Valley, citing rising costs, taxes, and regulation on families and small businesses.
priorities.quote: I am watching the place I call home become increasingly unaffordable for the people who built it.

priorities.text: On accountability, says she would work to cut wasteful government spending and lower taxes for working families.
On opportunity, says she supports growth that benefits local communities, including good-paying jobs, small-business growth, and worker protections in the AI economy.
priorities.quote: The Hudson Valley deserves more than data centers and empty promises.

statements.quote: I fully support ICE doing its job and removing criminal, illegal immigrants who threaten our communities.
statements.context: In a July 9, 2026 campaign statement on a proposed ICE facility in Newburgh

statements.quote: We should be empowering parents and students with more options, not fewer.
statements.context: In a May 11, 2026 campaign press release praising New York's participation in the federal Education Freedom Tax Credit

statements.quote: I will support a rational, all-of-the-above energy policy that includes natural gas, nuclear power, hydropower and renewables — prioritizing reliability and affordability instead of costly political mandates.
statements.context: In a statement to the Daily Freeman candidate form, Oct. 3, 2026

researchNotes: Auringer's campaign website (winwithjackie.com) was reachable on this pass and supplied biography and priorities above; she still has not completed a Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey and her Ballotpedia page has no independent biography section. Pass 2 (Oct. 2026): her campaign press releases and Daily Freeman coverage supplied three issue statements (immigration enforcement, school choice, energy); none squarely takes a side on the guide's statements, so no stances are listed. No statements found on abortion, guns, rent, taxes on high earners, tariffs or the other issues. Ryan has not stated detailed 2026 policy priorities on his Ballotpedia page or a reachable campaign/official site as of research date; his entry relies on biography, committee assignments, and election history. Auringer's campaign website gives no birth year, graduation year or employer name, so her biography is limited to what it states.
